REPORT
Date August 3, 1937.
Subject. National salvation Leaders Released.
Made by. D.I. Pan Lien-pih Forwarded by. C. Simpson
The seven national salvation leaders, Messrs.
Sung Chun-dz, Tsang Nai-chi, So Chien Li, Li Kung Poh, Tseu
Tao Fung, Wong Zao Dz and Miss Sz Lieng, who have been under
detention since November 23, 1936, on a charge of being
reactionaries, were released on bail on July 31, 1937. They
arrived here from Soochow by rail at 11.30 a.m. August 1,
and were welcomed by some 30 relatives and intimate friends
at the Shanghai North Railway Station.
At 1.15 p.m. August 1, these seven people were
entertained to luncheon at the Dinty Moore Restaurant, No.35
Ningpo Road, by some fifty persons, including Messrs. Tsang
Ts-zang (張志讓), lawyer, Pang Vung-ying (彭文應), professor
of the Shanghai Law College, who claimed to be the
representative of the various local national salvation
associations. A small number of students from the Liang
Zai Supplementary School, Continental Emporium Building,
Nanking Road, also attended the luncheon. Speeches were
delivered by the seven guests in which they asserted that
they would continue their efforts in the cause of national
salvation and what the organization stood for.
At 3.20 p.m. the lunchoen finished and the students
of the Liang Zai Supplementary School took their departure,
the remaining people, composed of relatives and friends, staying
to dinner in the Restaurant.
At 11 p.m. August 2, the seven national salvation
leaders left Shanghai for Nanking by rail to receive their
instructions from the National Government.
Pan Lien-pih

THE CHINA PRESS, MONDAY, AUGUST 2, 1937
23293

7 Salvationist
Leaders Here
From Soochow

Big Welcome Given
Group Long Held
In Prison

AWAIT REPLY
FROM CHIANG

Shen Chun-ju Looks
Pale; Miss Liang
Gained Weight

Looking none the worse for their eight-month detention in Soochow since last December, the seven All-Chinese National Salvation Association leaders, whose arrest last year caused a sensation in Shanghai, arrived here from Soochow at eleven o'clock yesterday morning.

The seven Salvationist leaders, headed by Mr. Shen Chun-ju, aged lawyer, were released on bail by the Soochow high court Saturday. It was announced that they would proceed to Nanking first before returning to Shanghai, and their unexpected arrive here yesterday morning was known to only a few of their relatives and friends beforehand.

Stepping off their train, the Salvationists found that a large crowd of their local followers were waiting at the station to welcome them. On the station platform, they spoke briefly and joined in shouting patriotic slogans.

Not Dampen Patriotism

At 1 o'clock, the seven salvation leaders, whose case for allegedly attempting to undermine the security of the state is still pending before the High Court, were entertained at luncheon, at which some 330 people were present. In turn, the seven guests of honor spoke, pledging that their arrest and long detention will not put a damper on their active patriotism.

Mr. Shen, the oldest member of the group who wears a bushy black beard and goatee, was looking slightly pale. He was dressed in a white linen gown, while his companions were attired in foreign clothes.

Miss Sze Liang, well-known local woman lawyer, appeared to have added some weight during her eight-month stay in the detention house. She was wearing a natty foreign style dress made of Chinese cotton material.

Shortly after their arrival, a joint statement was issued to the press, which revealed that they were waiting for a reply wire from Gen. Chiang Kai-shek, President of the Executive Yuan, before proceeding to Nanking. A telegram was sent to the Generalissimo immediately after they were released from the detention house in Soochow, asking for an interview.

Commenting on the current situation, the Salvationists were of the belief that two major issues now confront the nation: national consolidation and resistance against Japan.

They believe that under the guidance of the Central Government, a momentous war for China's racial independence will be fought, in which the final victory will be on the Chinese side.

June 14, 1937.

NIPRO

VARIOUS CIRCLES NATIONAL SALVATION ASSOCIATION
HOLDS DEMONSTRATION IN FRENCH CONCESSION

On June 12 the Kiangsu High
Court held the second hearing of the case against the seven
leaders of the national salvation movement.
The Shanghai Various Circles
National Salvation Association issued a notification to
various public bodies in Shanghai to the effect that at
3 p.m. June 13 a demonstration would be held on a piece of
vacant ground on Route de Zikawei, French Concession, to
demand the release of the seven arrested leaders. About
5000 students and labourers assembled at the appointed
time and held a demonstration under a presiding board of
five professors.
Acting on information, the French
Police dispatched a number of policemen to the scene to deal
with the situation.
The chairman of the demonstration
, during the course of his speech, said that the seven leaders
were reported to have been sentenced to 5 years' imprisonment,
He further said that if such patriots were to be condemned
all Chinese people would be condemned because of their love
of patriotic movements. For this reason, the people
should strongly demand the release of the seven leaders.
This speech was followed by a loud cry from the 5000
demonstrators that the Government should release the seven
leaders immediately.
The following resolutions were
passed:-
1. That the trial of the seven leaders be cancelled and
the prisoners released immediately.
2. That patriotic movements be protected.
3. That the freedom of speech and organization be protected.
4. That democratic administration be practised.
5. That all political prisoners be released.
6. That Japanese goods be boycotted and smuggling be
suppressed by armed force.
7. That the Government be supported and an anti-Japanese
front be formed immediately.
8. That the East Hopei Autonomous Government be cancelled
and the lost territory be recovered.
9. That China's entire population be armed and stirred up.
10. That the Government issue an order to the people to
organize national salvation associations.
11. That the Government should finance the North-East
University.
12. That diplomatic affairs be open to the public.
13. That all pro-Japanese government officers be dismissed.
The demonstration was dispersed at 5 p.m. due to the
rain and the efforts of the French Police.
A large number of inflammatory anti-Japanese handbills
were distributed among the demonstrators.
The handbill contains the following
slogans:-
1. The Government should unite with the people to resist
enemies and save the country.
2. Celebrate in advance the release of the seven leaders
and the release of political prisoners.
3. Arrest of patriots must be discontinued and patriotic
movements must not be interfered with.
4. Freedom and equality of the people must be practised and
national independence must be completed.
5. Hurrah for the freedom, equality and independence of
China!

On November 26 Detectives from P.S.B. in cooperation with French Police raided house No. 21 Route Jupleix with a warrant for the arrest of one Tang Chien Sung (湯堅松) on a charge of being a Communist. It appears that Yao was a Government spy on the "patriotic movement" in the pay of Mr. Chang Chung Ming (張仲明), a special delegate of the Central Tangpu, and he was required to give evidence against Tsang Nai Chee, one of the leaders recently arrested in connection with the national salvation movement, but as he had refused to do so, the P.S.B. took out a warrant for his arrest. The case is still pending in the French Special District Court. It is doubtful whether the P.S.B. will be able to produce evidence of Yao being a Communist and establish a prima facie case against him. It is alleged by the P.S.B. that Yao was implicated in a statement made by an arrested Communist but this cannot be confirmed.

Manifesto of the Illegally Arrested Sung Chun Dz and
Six Others Support Committee

Brethren throughout the country; we wish to tell you
one tragic incident as follows :-

When the Japanese imperialists are using gas and bombs
to invade our Suiyuan province and the nation is on the verge of
destruction, and the people are about to become slaves, the
Chinese Government, instead of fighting against the Japanese, took
into custody seven leaders of the national salvation associations
on the evening of November 23.

The government authorities declare that the people should
not meddle in politics and that if they do, they will be regarded
as reactionary elements or communists.

Brethren, is the attitude of the government right? Are
Sung Chun Dz, Wong Shao Dz, Soo Chi Li, and Sze Liang, who are
lawyers, Li Kung Poh, who is the principal of the Liang Zai
Supplementary School, Tsang Nai Chi, who is a famous banker, and
Chen Tao Feng, who is a noted writer, bandits or communists?

The attitude adopted by these people, which is the
attitude of the national salvation associations towards national
salvation is that since the fate of China is in the balance and
the country is about to be conquered by the Japanese imperialists,
the Chinese people, irrespective of officials or civilians, rich men
or poor, and party affiliations, who do not wish to become running
dogs of the Japanese, must unite and oppose Japan and the Chinese
traitors. Since the foundation of the national salvation
associations, their activities and those of the seven arrested
persons are open to the people of the country.

Brethren, is the attitude of the arrested persons and the
national salvation associations wrong? Must not the Chinese people
save their own country? Must the Chinese people be the running
dogs of the Japanese? Must the Chinese people slaughter
themselves?

If the attitude taken by the arrested persons is right,
why have the government authorities arrested them? Is it that the
people who wish to save their country are communists?

Brethren, China belongs to the people, every one who has
a right to save his nation. We want to save the country and we
resolutely demand that the government release the seven arrested
and assure us of the freedom of conducting the national salvation
movement.

Brethren, we wish to make known the arrest of the seven
leaders as far as possible in order that the people may render
them assistance and save the nation.

November 24.

政府當局說：國事不准他們管，他們救國，就是反動份子，是共產黨。
同胞們，這些話對嗎？做律師的沈鈞儒，王造時，沙千里，史良；和量才補習學校
校長李公樸，有名的銀行家章乃器，有名的著作家鄒韜奮，這些人，請問你，會做土匪
共產黨嗎？
他們平日所主張的，（也就是救國會所主張的）是：中國已經到了最危險的時候，
快要給日本帝國主義滅亡了。中國人民，不管是大官員和小百姓，不管是有錢的和窮光
蛋，不管那一黨那一派，只要不願意作東洋人的奴狗，都要聯合起來反抗東洋人和賣國
賊。自從救國會成立以來，救國會的言論行動和這七位的言論行動，很明白的擺在全國
人民的面前：完全是根據上面的主張的。
同胞們！他們的主張錯了嗎？中國人不應該救中國嗎？中國人應該做東洋人的奴狗
嗎？中國人應該自己人殺自己人嗎？
如果他們的主張是對的，那麼，政府當局捉他們去，是什麼理由呢？說救國就是共
產黨嗎？
同胞們！中國是大家的，誰都可以救國，救國是絕對自由的。我們為了要救國家，
我們堅決的要求政府馬上釋放這七位領袖！保證以後救國
運動的自由！
同胞們！我們要把這個事變，廣汎的傳播，大家起來援助我們的領袖，挽救
我們的國家！

hurriedly owing to the presence of several members of the

Municipal Police.

Translation of French Police Report dated November 23, 1936

Arrest at the request of the Chinese Authorities of three
directors of the National Salvation Federation of Various Circles.

At 9 p.m. on November 22, Dr HUNG CHI (洪起)? Chief of the
2nd Branch of the Public Safety Bureau advised us by telephone
that the Mayor of Shanghai had received orders from Nanking to
arrest the directors of the clandestine anti-Japanese Association
known as "The Federation of the various circles for National
Salvation" (上海各界救国联合会). At the same time he requested our
assistance in effecting certain of these arrests in the French
Concession.

At about 11 p.m. he delivered to us official letter "Te" 298,
a translation of which is attached herewith.

By this letter and the list attached, the Chinese Authorities
requested us to effect the arrest with a view to subsequent
extradition of the persons named hereafter :

Mr TSANG NAI CHI (章乃器), Shi Wei Chun, Route Delastre,
formerly one of the directors of the Chekiang Industrial Bank,
150 Hankow Road. Promoter of the Federation of the various circles
of Shanghai for National Salvation. Chief of the intellectuals
circles group "United Front of Left Wing Revolutionaries
(左派人民革命联合阵线), organised with the object of confronting the
Japanese menace by the different political parties of the Kuomintang
except : Neo-Kuomintang, Nationalist, Communist, Productive,
Socialist-Democratic, etc... (Report 2541/R). Participated in the
May 30, 1936 demonstration. Was one of the members of the Presidium
of this demonstration (1133/B). Presided over the meeting held on
January 28, 1936 at the Chamber of Commerce in commemoration of
the anniversary of the Sino-Japanese incidents of 1932, and led the
cortege which crossed the International Settlement in order to
visit the tomb of the unknown heroes (1510/1). Member of the
Administrative Council of the Chinese Physical Culture Association,
No.92 Rue Hue, organised with the object of favouring in China the

(2)

practise of sports, and more especially, Chinese boxing (Report
593/1). Member of the Administrative Council of "The Bankers'
Cooperative Credit Service Ltd.", 133 Yuen King Yuen Road (Report
584/1). Member of the Neo-Kuomintang Party (Report 1159/S).

Miss SZE LIANG (史良), No.1 Lafayette Terrace, advocate,
Chief of the Women's Section of the "United Front of Left wing
Revolutionaries. Editor of the clandestine publication "Journal
of National Salvation (Report 114/3). Took part in the May 30, 1936
demonstration. Was one of the members of the Presidium of this
demonstration (vide Report 1133/S). President of the Feminine
Association of Shanghai for National Salvation (pro-communist
organisation) (Report No.1007/S), the correspondence office of
which was installed at No.55 Yuen King Yuen Road (Cf. Report 1589/1).
Presided over the meeting held on March 8, 1936, international
day of women at the Y.M.C.A., No.599 Szechuen Road. At the issue
of this meeting certain communist elements suggested that a
demonstration be held in the streets. This proposal was approved
and the demonstrators left Szechuen Road and went to Nantao via
Rue Tourane ( The Reserve Unit of the French Police had to intervene
and during the struggle which ensued two persons were injured -
Report 1589/1). Pleaded especially on behalf of communists who
were being prosecuted (Report 1485/1. Presided over the meeting
held on January 28, 1936 at the Chamber of Commerce in commemoration
of the 1932 Sino-Japanese incidents and headed the cortège which
traversed the International Settlement in order to visit the tomb
of the unknown heroes (Report 1510/1). Was a member of the Society
for the defense of the citizens against foreign invasion, organized
in the beginning of February 1933, the secret office of which was
located in the French Concession; first at No.48 Route Vallon and
later at No.6, Passage 68 of the same street (Cf. Report 83/R).

Mr CHOW TAO FENG alias CHOW HENKING (鄒韜奮 鄒恩潤 ),
No.4, Passage 601 Rue Lafayette. Graduate of St John's University,

(3)
ex-Director of the Sen-Huo book-store (Life) (生活書店), ex-editor
of the old revues Sen-Huo (Life) (生活週刊), Ta Chung Seng Huo
(Popular Life) (大衆生活), Eternal Life (永生週刊) and founder
of the journal Sen Huo Jhih Pao (生活日報), published in Hongkong
which has stopped publication. Editor and publisher of the weekly
edition SEN HUO, the office of which is at Office 319 in the
"Shanghai Times" building, 160 Avenue Edward VII. Was one of the
founder members of the Chinese Society of the Rights of Man
League, an association dissolved in 1933 by order of the Chinese
authorities. Now a member of the Nationalist Party (Kuo Chia Chu
I Pai) (國民黨左派), directed by General FENG YU HSIANG and
General LI LIEH CHUN, which is at the head of the anti-Japanese
movement. In 1935 CHOW founded the revue "Life". Following the
Sino-Japanese hostilities in 1932, this revue having taken on a
purely anti-Chiang Kai Shek character, the Generalissimo
ordered the local authorities to ban sale of it. When Mr CHOW
heard of this order he found it preferable to go on a voyage to
Europe and entrusted the management of his revue to HSU PAH CHING
(徐伯昕). As the revue continued to publish numerous articles
against the National Government, a search was carried out at the
office of the publication at the request of the Chinese authorities
on December 11, 1933. Following this raid the director decided to
suspend publication of "Life". After a long sojourn in Europe,
chiefly in the U.S.S.R., Mr CHOW returned to Shanghai in the
Spring of 1935 and founded with the support of General LI LIEH
CHUN his revue "Popular Life" (大衆生活), a revue which, beyond
doubt, is the propaganda organ of the anti-Japanese faction of
the Kuomintang Party (Cf Report 1512/1).

The required arrests were carried out between 2 and 3 a.m.
at the homes of the accused.

At the home of CHOW TAO FENG (韜奮) some thirty brochures
and circulars without much interest were found. Some of the
foreign
brochures in foreign languages are the work of known communists.

At the home of TSANG HAI CHI (章乃器) were seized 4,000
pamphlets in favour of the strikers of Japanese mills and

(4)
subscriptions opened by a Committee of Assistance to the Strikers,
44 books of tickets with counterfoils, each containing 50 tickets,
for subscriptions on behalf of the strikers, 6 copies of Bulletin
No.1 of information from the "Federation of Chinese Students for
National Salvation (学界救国联合会).
At Mis SZE LIANG's place some regulations appertaining to
the "Committee of Aid to the soldiers opposing the Enemy" and some
documents without interest were seized.
On being interrogated by the Political Branch the three
prisoners denied the accusation of communist activities, but admitted
anti-Japanese activities.
In the International Settlement, at the same time and under
the same circumstances, the following persons belonging to the
same organisation were arrested :
Mr LI KUNG PO (李公樸)/ Director of the Liang Zai School
(量才補習学校) in Nanking Road, Continental Emporium, Nanking; director
of the SHUN PAO Library; editor of the revue "The life of Students";
member of the administrative committee of the Shanghai section
for Sino-Soviet cultural cooperation, the office of which is at
the University of Communications, Avenue Haig. Member of the left
wing of the United Revolutionaries. Has participated in various
anti-Japanese and anti-government demonstrations.
Mr SHA CHUAN LI (沙千里), a lawyer with offices at 429 Kiukiang
Road. Editor of the bi-monthly revue Seng Fu Tse Se (生活知識)
(Shengroxhsh), No.3 Passage 512 Chengtu Rd; not very well known.
Mr WANG CHAO JU (王造時), advocate, one of the promoters
of the Association of various circles of Shanghai for National
Salvation. Member of the Party Neo-Kuomintang. Member of the
educational association of the Shanghai district (organisation
with social democratic tendencies); member of the Chinese Social
Democratic Party. Professor at the Kwang Hua University in Great
Western Road. Very active member of the League for the defense of
Civic Rights - President TSAI YUAN PEI (蔡元培). Took part in the
manifestation of May 30, 1936 and that of January 28, 1936.

(5)

Belonged to the group "United Front of the Revolutionaries of the
Left Wing."

Mr SHEI CHUNG SHU (沈鈞儒) alias SHEN HENG SHAN (沈衡山),
member of the Permanent Committee of the Shanghai Bar (Association).
His chambers are located at No.6 Tatung Li, Burkill Road. Rector
of the Kwangwan Law Institute; one of the promoters of the
Federation of Various Circles for National Salvation; member of
the group "United Front of Left Wing Revolutionaries." Has taken
part in various anti-Japanese and anti-Government demonstrations.

The Police Force of the French

I have the honour to inform you confidenti-
ally that according to information received by us, one TCHANG NGAI
HSI ( 张 乃 器 ) and two others, who have secretly accepted to work

the territory of the Municipality (Chinese) of Shanghai all kinds
of workers and students movements in order to hinder the public
peace, and with the object of creating disorders the consequences
of which are likely to be serious and of committing acts of
violence etc...

of these individuals, TCHANG NGAI HSI and consorts, known as
professional agitators occupied in grouping extremist elements,
in propagating communist doctrines, and in fomenting insurrect-
ionary conspiracies. At present they are pursuing their subversive
activities and unless they are immediately placed in a position
where they can do no harm, no one knows what may be the consequences
of their agitation.

In consequence, the bearer will hand over to
you the present letter and attached list, and I beg that you
to
will accord us the necessary assistance to enable the arrests to
be proceeded with and the subsequent extradition of the accused
effected.

(signed) TSAI CHING CHUN
Head of the Public Safety Bureau

of the 1932 Sino-Japanese incidents and headed the cortege which
traversed the International Settlement in order to visit the tomb
of the unknown heroes (Report 1510/1). Was a member of the Society
for the defense of the citizens against foreign invasion, organized
in the beginning of February 1933, the secret office of which was
located in the French Concession; first at No.48 Route Vallon and
later at No.6, Passage 68 of the same street (Cf. Report 85/A).

Mr CHOW TAO FENG alias CHOW HSIENSHENG (邹韬奋 邹恩润),
No.4, Passage 601 Rue Lafayette. Graduate of St John's University,

(3)
ex-Director of the Sen-Huo book-store (Life) (生活書店), ex-editor
of the old revues Sen-Huo (Life) (生活週刊), Ta Chun Seng Huo
(Popular Life) 大眾生活, Eternal Life 永生週刊 and founder
of the journal Sen Huo Jhih Pao (生活日報), published in Hongkong
which has stopped publication. Editor and publisher of the weekly
edition SEN HUO, the office of which is at Office 319 in the
"Shanghai Times building, 160 Avenue Edward VII. Was one of the
founder members of the Chinese Society of the Rights of Man
League, an association dissolved in 1933 by order of the Chinese
authorities. Now a member of the Nationalist Party (Kuo Chia Chu
I Pai) (國家主義派), directed by General FENG YU HSIANG and
General LI LIEH CHUN, which is at the head of the anti-Japanese
movement. In 1935 CHOW founded the revue "Life". Following the
Sino-Japanese hostilities in 1932, this revue having taken on a
purely anti-Chiang Kai Shek character, the Generalissimo
ordered the local authorities to ban sale of it. When Mr CHOW
heard of this order he found it preferable to go on a voyage to
Europe and entrusted the management of his revue to HSU PO CHING
(徐伯昕). As the revue continued to publish numerous articles
against the National Government, a search was carried out at the
office of the publication at the request of the Chinese authorities
on December 11, 1933. Following this raid the director decided to
suspend publication of "Life". After a long sojourn in Europe,
chiefly in the U.S.S.R., Mr CHOW returned to Shanghai in the
Spring of 1935 and founded with the support of General LI LIEH
CHUN his revue "Popular Life" 大眾生活, a revue which, beyond
doubt, is the propaganda organ of the anti-Japanese faction of
the Kuomintang Party (Cf Report 1512/1).
The required arrests were carried out between 2 and 3 a.m.
at the homes of the accused.
At the home of CHOW TAO FENG (周韜奮) some thirty brochures
and circulars without much interest were found. Some of the
foreign
brochures in foreign languages are the work of known communists.
At the home of TSANG HAI CHI (章乃器) were seized 4,000
pamphlets in favour of the strikers of Japanese mills and

(4)
subscriptions opened by a Committee of Assistance to the Strikers,
44 books of tickets with counterfoils, each containing 50 tickets,
for subscriptions on behalf of the strikers, 6 copies of Bulletin
No.1 of information from the "Federation of Chinese Students for
National Salvation (学生救国联合会).
At Miss SZE LI NG's place some regulations appertaining to
the "Committee of Aid to the soldiers opposing the Enemy" and some
documents without interest were seized.
On being interrogated by the Political Branch the three
prisoners denied the accusation of communist activities, but admitted
anti-Japanese activities.
In the International Settlement, at the same time and under
the same circumstances, the following persons belonging to the
same organisation were arrested :

where they can do no harm, no one knows what may be the consequences
of their agitation.

REPORT OF POLICE INVESTIGATIONS.
The following is the statement of. Li Kung Po ( 李公樸 ), age 35,
native of Changchow taken by me D.S. Kelly
at B'Well Stn on the 23/11/36 and interpreted by ------.

My name is Li Kung Po ( 李公樸 ), age 35, married,
native of Changchow, residing House 24, Lane 1376 Yu Yuen Road.
I arrived in Shanghai 5 years ago from Nanking to obtain
a situation with the "Shun Pao" Chinese Press on Hankow Road
as an editor and to organise a library and the Shun Pao
evening classes, where I have been employed since my arrival
at a salary of $300.00 per month.
I am not a member of any political party and have no
communist feelings. My last political connections were in
the year 1927 when I proceeded to the United States of
America where I studied politics and for two years until 1929
when I returned to Nanking and obtained a situation with the
Official Moral Endeavour Association until I left for Shanghai
as stated. My salary from the Association was $200.00 per
month.
I have numerous friends in Shanghai whom I have met during
my sojourn here.
This is my true statement.

Signed and crossmarked by:
Li Kung Po.

The following is the statement of Sung Chun Zu ( ), age 63,

My name is Sung Chun Zu, age 63, native of Kashing,
residing 51, Lane 1292 Yu Yuen Road, where I have resided

I came to Shanghai 9 years ago from Hangchow (1927) and
I have followed my employment as a lawyer since my arrival,
and I am a member of the Chinese Lawyer's Association, Rue
Lafayette.

Previous to come to Shanghai I was a member of the
Chekiang Provincial Government between 1926 and 1927, having
arrived in Hangchow from Peking in the year 1926.

Previous to the year 1926 I was a member of the National
Parliament in Peking since the forming of the Kuomintang
Government in 1911.

My reasons for coming to Shanghai was I had to seek
employment when the Provincial Government of Chekiang
reorganized in 1927.

I am at present a member of the Kuomintang Political
Party but take no active part.

I have numerous friends and relatives in Shanghai, many
of whom are members of the Kuomintang Party.

This is my true statement.

SHANGHAI EVENING POST & MERCURY.
FEB 9 - 1939

“Seven Gentlemen” Going Free

Chungking Court
Withdraws Case

Activities Of Pre-War
Period No Longer
Subversive

The famous “Seven Gentlemen Case,” in which seven leaders of the National Salvation Association were charged with subversive activities endangering the Chinese Republic, has been brought to a conclusion in Chungking.

Declaring that the views and actions of the seven scholars, lawyers and professors were in no way contrary to the present national policy, the Chungking High Court, assigned by the Highest Court to take over the case from the Soochow Branch Kiangsu High Court, withdrew the prosecution against them. The decision was given in Chungking in the absence of the accused who are now actively engaged in political training and war service duties. Several of them are members of the People’s Political Council.

The seven leaders of the All-China National Salvation Association, an organisation with a large following among students and workers, are: Shen Chung-ju, lawyer; Li Kung-po, writer; Seh Chien-li, lawyer; Tsang Nai-chi, economist; Taou Tao-fen, writer; Wang Chao-shih, professor; and Miss Shih Liang, woman lawyer.

In the spring of 1937, they were rounded up in Shanghai and sent to Soochow to stand trial on charges of subversive activities. Demonstrations followed their arrest and, led by Madame Sun Yat-sen, widow of the late founder of the Kuomintang, many stormed the Soochow court. The legal battle lasted many months but came to an abrupt end in July when they were released following the outbreak of hostilities in North China. The ruling by the Chungking Court was merely a formality upholding their views and actions.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Tuesday, July 6, 1937

Mme. Sun Active
Convicting Self
Widow And Colleagues
Collecting Evidence
To Get Into Jail

Madame Sun Yat-sen, widow of the late founder of the Kuomintang and "father" of the Chinese republic, and her colleagues are today collecting evidence against themselves in order that they may be detained and prosecuted with the seven All-China National Salvation Association leaders now facing charges of undermining the security of the state in the Kiangsu High Court in Soochow.

The party of 12, including Mrs. Chang Nai-chi, wife of one of the seven prisoners in Soochow, returned to Shanghai last night by the afternoon express after having staged a 10-hour "sit-down" strike in the Soochow court during which they demanded detention and prosecution with the seven accused inasmuch as they are co-workers in the National Salvation Association.

It was finally agreed that the 12 should furnish the procurate of the Kiangsu High Court with evidence substantiating their claim that they are similar in belief and behavior with the seven All-China National Salvation Association leaders.

The party arrived at the court shortly after 9 o'clock yesterday morning. They engaged in a heated verbal clash with the president and chief procurator of the court and were left alone in the reception room at 12.30. It was not until 5 p.m. that a procurator appeared and resumed negotiations with the petitioners. During the interval, however, the court supplied the petitioners with electric fans, tea and towels.

The discussion between the petitioners and the procurator lasted for more than two hours during which the latter is said to have admitted that the National Salvation Association itself is not an illegal organization and promised the petitioners to detain them and prosecute them in the event they produce sufficient evidence against themselves.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Monday, July 5, 1937

Mme. Sun Stages
Sit-Down Strike
In Soochow Court

Widow Of Party Chief
And Others Seek
Arrest, Trial

TRIBUNAL REJECTS
SYMPATHY PLEA

Over 200 Said Asking
To Share Charges
With 7 Leaders

(Special To The Post)
SOOCHOW, July 5.—Madame Sun Yat-sen, widow of the founder of the Kuomintang and "father" of the Chinese Republic, has declared a "sit-down" strike in the Kiangsu High Court here.
With eleven others, who described themselves as co-workers of the seven All-China National Salvation Association leaders now facing charges of undermining the security of the state in the tribunal, Madame Sun, who is the former Miss Soong Ching-ling, a sister of of Madame Chiang Kai-shek and Madame H. H. Kung, arrived here by the "Capital Express" from Shanghai this morning.

See President
They immediately proceeded to the court where they demanded to see the president and the chief procurator of the court to present a petition urging that they be also detained with the seven National Salvation Association leaders because they are similar both in "belief and behavior." They should share the consequences with the seven for what they have done together, they declared.
A delegation of three, headed by Madame Sun, was finally allowed to meet the president of the court. During the interview the president claimed that he has no rights to order their detention and that a procurators' conference must be called to deal with the request. The chief procurator finally came to meet Madame Sun, Mr. Hu Yutsz and Mr. Chu Ching-lai, writers.

Better Go Home
A heated verbal clash took place at this moment. The procurator declared he has no right to detain them and that in his investigations, he has so far found nothing against the petitioners warranting their detention and prosecution. The weather is hot in Soochow and the petitioners had better return to Shanghai immediately, the chief procurator said.
The argument continued until 12 noon when the chief procurator left the reception room. As the court is observing a summer schedule, no responsible officials were to show up this afternoon.

Have Tiffin
Undaunted by the refusal to detain them and to prosecute them together with the seven accused on charges of undermining the security of the state, Madame Sun and her colleagues decided to remain inside the reception room. Bowls of noodles were ordered and sent to the reception room as their "tiffin." At an early hour this afternoon, they were showing no signs of leaving.
Some 50 youths were waiting outside the court compound with a similar request that they be arrested and prosecuted together with the "seven gentlemen," as the seven accused are known. It is said that more were arriving for the same purpose.

No Date Set
The 12 petitioners who arrived this morning, other than Madame Sun, Mr. Hu and Mr. Chu, included Mrs. Chang Nai-chi, wife of the economist who is held as one of the seven leaders of the National Salvation Association.
No date for the resumption of the trial of the seven now world-famous "salvationists," however, has been set. It is widely rumored that they are due for release on bail and that they will go abroad. Their case, it is understood, will be widely discussed during the Kuling conference of Chinese intellectuals when they meet under the chairmanship of General Chiang Kai-shek and Mr. Wang Ching-wei, beginning July 15.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Saturday, June 26, 1937

Patriots Demand
Arrest For Aid
To Salvationists

Liberal Leaders Urge
Own Trial; Petition
Sent To Soochow

“IS PATRIOTISM
CRIME IN CHINA?”

Verbal Clashes Mark
Session; Hearing
Postponed

Declaring that they are also directors, members and friends of the All-China National Salvation Association and that they had worked together for the same cause with the seven accused now facing the serious charge of undermining the security of the state, Madame Sun Yat-sen, widow of the late founder of the Kuomintang and father” of the Chinese republic, Madame Liao Chung-kai, widow of the late Kuomintang leader assassinated in Canton in 1925, and 11 professors, authors and movie stars yesterday filed a petition with the Kiangsu High Court in Soochow asking that they also be placed under arrest and share the punishment, if any is forthcoming, with the seven defendants.

Those who signed the petition, which formed another dramatic development in the so-called “Case of the Seven Gentlemen,” are: Madame Sun (the former Miss Soong Ching-ling), Madame Liao, Professors Chu Ching-lai, Peng Wen-yin, Chang Tsung-hsi, Wang Puh-yen, Chang Chung-shih and Pan Ta-kwei, Writers Yu-chih, Wong Tung-shan, Chiang Tien-yih and Chen Tu-chiu, and Movie Actress Chen Po-chen, the “stormy-petrel of Chinese freedom” who last year was “requested” to leave Peiping due to Japanese resentment over her activities in organizing an anti-Japanese movement in the former capital.

Translation
A free translation of the full text of the petition follows:
“In connection with the case agains Shen Chung-ju et al on charges of endangering the republic, the petitioners, whose opinions and behavior are similar to theirs, pledge themselves to the court for trial in the same case.
“It needs little explanation that it is not a crime to be patriotic. The activities of Shen Chung-ju et al in working for the cause of national salvation are not illegal. Now they have been detained for more than half-a-year. If they were found guilty, the entire nation would be agog. The petitioners are either members of the National Salvation Association or directors of the National Salvation Association or, despite their non-membership, have worked together in the past with Shen et al for the cause of national salvation.

Ask Same Treatment
“If to be patriotic is a crime, then the petitioners should be given the same treatment as Shen et al. The petitioners could not allow Shen et al to take the punishment but are willing to share the responsibility resulting from the joint activities for the cause of national salvation. We urge the court to put us under detention for trial. In the event that to be patriotic is not a crime, we shall regain our freedom with Shen et al. If to be patriotic is a crime, we shall share the punishment with Shen et al. We are willing to risk our bodies to test if to be patriotic is a crime or not.”

Verbal clashes between Procurator Ong Chan-hien who drew up the indictment and the defendants and their defense lawyers and the persistent requests by the defense that evidence and witnesses in their favor be taken into consideration featured the lengthy seven-hour session in the Kiangsu High Court yesterday. The clashes developed to such a climax that the procurator threatened to take disciplinary action against the defense counsels and the defendants only to find his statement receiving a further deluge of scathing denunciations.

Coup Discussed
A major section of the hearing was devoted to the questioning of the accused in connection with their alleged instigation of the Sian Coup. The charges caused a deluge of protest from the defendants who urged the court to summon General Chang Hsueh-liang to the court for questioning whether he had staged the coup at their instigation or at his own will. They also suggested that the court also question Mr. Ma Hsiang-po, the 98-year-old member of the State Council, General Sung Che-yuan, chairman of the Hopei-Chahar Political Council, General Han Fu-chu, chairman of the Shantung provincial Government, and General Fu Tso-yi, chairman of the Suiyuan provincial government, concerning the identic telegrams despatched by the National Salvation Association asking them to send troops to Suiyuan to aid the defense against the “Manchukuan” and Mongolian insurgents.

The court rejected all of the requests but agreed to take steps to obtain the files from the Military Affairs Commission in connection with General Chang Hsueh-liang’s trial for the coup for which he was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment, a sentence subsequently lifted.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Tuesday, June 15, 1937

Seven-Gentlemen
Release Sought
By Many Leaders

Financiers, Publishers
Here Urge Freedom
Of Salvationists

SCHEME STUDIED
FOR COMPROMISE

Prisoners Might Leave
China; Nipponese
Attack Trial

The movement for the release, unconditionally or otherwise, of the seven All-China National Salvation Association leaders now detained in Soochow on charges of undermining the security of the state is rapidly growing.

More than 10 leading Chinese figures in Shanghai financial circles have jointly telegraphed to Chairman Lin Sen of the National Government, Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, Mr. Wang Ching-wei and President Onli Cheng of the Judicial Yuan asking for leniency for Mr. Chang Nai-chi, one of the "Seven Gentlemen," and his release.

Mr. Chang, banker and economist, the financial leaders pleaded, worked in the financial world for more than 10 years and his services for works on economic reconstruction should be valuable. The names appearing on the telegram included those of Messrs. S. I. Hsu, Li Ming, Ling Hong-mou, Tzeng Yang-shih and Yu Kuo-ching.

The Publishers' Association in Shanghai is also rallying to the aid of its distinguished member, Mr. Tsou Tao-fan, writer and editor who once was publisher of the now defunct "Life Weekly." In a telegram worded in the same manner, the Association urged the high authorities to release the seven.

Conditional Release Talked

Two influential Chinese community leaders, at the same time, are quietly asserting their efforts for the same end via a different route. They are Messrs. Tu Yueh-sen, president of the Shanghai Civic Association, and Mr. Y. M. Chien, manager of the Joint Savings Bank. They visited Soochow during the week-end and are understood to have discussed with the seven accused a proposal to arrange for their release under conditions acceptable both to the Nanking authorities and the defendants.

Details of the reported proposal, however, could not be ascertained this morning. It is rumored, however, that a telegram has already been sent to Nanking by the two community leaders and new developments may take place within the next few days. It is generally believed that the "Seven Gentlemen" would be required to suspend their activities and, perhaps, go abroad in the event they are dismissed from the charges.

Ruling Delayed

Meanwhile, the Kiangsu High Court in Soochow has telegraphed to the Ministry of Justice for instructions in connection with the petitions filed by the seven now world-famous defendants for new judges to preside over their trial. The Ministry of Justice is understood to have replied that the court is entitled to the right to give a ruling on the petition and that in the event the accused are not satisfied with the decision, they may file an appeal with the Supreme Court.

No date has yet been set for the resumption of the trial. The question arising out of the petition for new judges on grounds that the three judges who presided over the first session are allegedly prejudiced and biased must be first settled before the trial may proceed.

Trial A "Farce"

The trial of seven leaders of the All-China National Salvation Association in Soochow was described this morning by The Shanghai Mainichi as a "farce."

The accused men, the daily said, had a six-month respite to prepare their defense. Their replies at last Friday's session showed extreme caution.

Significance Said Lost

Moreover, the Mainichi declared the trial was shorn of all its significance by the reported compromise accord between the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party.

Finding support in this accord, the journal asserted, the defendants "actually put the Soochow judges on the defensive."

"It is interesting, however," the Mainichi concluded, "to see what verdict will be passed by the government without impairing its own dignity."

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Monday, April 26, 1937

Salvation Trial
Begins April 28
In High Tribune

Ten To Face Charges
Of Endangering
State Safety

TWO OUT ON BAIL
WITH 8 IN JAIL

Educational, Culture
Circles Watching
Proceedings

The trial of the 10 alleged leaders of the National Salvation Association, including the seven prominent intellectuals arrested in Shanghai November 23, will begin at the Kiangsu High Court in Soochow on Wednesday, April 28, it was announced today. The hearing, which will be continued on April 29, will be presided over by Chief Judge Fang Wen and Judges Chu Chien-hsen and Hai Wen.

The 10 accused are charged with offenses against the security of the state under Article Six of the Emergency Law governing Punishment for Offenses Endangering the Republic. When convicted, a maximum term of 15 years may be given. The minimum sentence, according to the article, is five years' imprisonment.

Two On Bail

Of the 10 accused, two are on bail and eight detained in the cells of the Kiangsu High Court. The seven arrested in Shanghai and among those detained are: Messrs. Shen Chung-ju, Sa Chien-li, Wong Tsao-shih, Li Kung-po, Tsing Nai-chi, Tsou Tao-fen and Miss Shih Liang. They are lawyers, professors, economists and writers. The other accused detained in the cells is Mr. Tso Tsing, formerly a secretary of the Chekiang Railway. He was arrested early this year in Nanking, where he is alleged to have attempted to organise an all-Kiangsu National Salvation Association.

The two accused released on bail and summoned to attend the trial on April 28 are Hu Liau-nsing and Ren Chung-kao, self-confessed members of the National Salvation Association. They were among the few delegates who signed a petition asking for the release of the seven prisoners. Few days ago they went to the court to present the petition, they were compelled to appear at witness stand and had to face the chief prosecutor. The three other delegates, however, did not attend. We hear that we still find them difficult to locate for their arrest has been ordered.

Seeks Professor

The court is also seeking the custody of Professor Tao Yin-chu, prominent Chinese rural education expert, whom the procurator charges as one of the leaders of the allegedly subversive organization. Professor Tao was known to have been lecturing in the United States.

The trial is being watched by Chinese educational and cultural circles and others sympathetic with their clamor for resistance against Japanese aggression. Only recently a group of American educators and editors, including Dr. John Dewey and Dr. Paul Monroe, cabled to Nanking expressing their concern over the arrest and detention of the seven National Salvation Association leaders.

General Li Lieh-chung, veteran Kuomintang member and a close associate of General Feng Yu-hsiang, yesterday visited the cells to call on the seven prisoners, according to Soochow reports. General Li has been staying in Soochow recently.

Salvationists
Facing Formal
Court Charges

Offenses To Security
Of State Alleged
By Government

TRIAL SCHEDULED
FOR THIS WEEK

Four More Well-Known
Intellectuals Named
As Conspirators

Formal charges of alleged offenses against the security of the state have been preferred against the seven leaders of the All-China National Salvation Association arrested in Shanghai on November 23, 1936, and three others who were taken into custody later. The trial of the 10 persons, including a woman lawyer, is scheduled to begin at the Kiangsu High Court in Soochow sometime this week.

The indictment against the "National Salvation" leaders, filed by the procurators with the High Court at the last minute before the expiration of the time-limit of the legally allowed detention of four months, also charged four others with similar offenses. As they are not yet within the jurisdiction of the High Court warrants were issued for their arrest. One of the "wanted" man is Mr. Tao Yin-chi, prominent educator and expert in rural education, who is known to be in America and last reported to be lecturing at Columbia University.

Jail Term Provided
The 10 accused now in custody of the Kiangsu High Court are charged with having organized groups with the aim of endangering the republic and having propagated doctrines incompatible with the Three Principles of the People. The article provides, in case of conviction, a jail term of from five to 15 years.

All of the 10 accused, it is understood, have denied the charges when they were handed duplicate copies of the indictment. They are consulting with their counsels to file their petitions.

Prisoners Well-Known
The names of the 10 accused of whom the first seven were arrested in the International Settlement and French Concession on November 23, follow:

1. Shen Chung-ju, lawyer, member of the standing committee of the Chinese Bar Association and dean of a law college in Shanghai.
2. Tsang Nai-chi, American-educated economist and formerly manager of a leading Chinese bank in Shanghai, being relieved of the post for his alleged political activities.
3. Li Kung-pe, American-educated educator and formerly president of the Sze Liang-tsai (newspaper publisher) Memorial School.
4. Tsou Tao-fen, writer and formerly editor of the Life Weekly, the periodical with the largest circulation in China.
5. Wang Tsou-shih, American-educated lawyer and formerly a professor with a local university.
6. Sa Chien-li, lawyer.
7. Miss Sze Liang, lawyer and the only woman in the group.
8. Lo Ching, formerly secretary at the Chengtai Railway Administration, arrested in Kiangyin last year and now detained in Soochow.
9 and 10. Ku Liu-hsing and Ren Chung-kao, alleged members of the Association retained since February 3 when attending a session in response to summons issued them by the High Court.

Warrants Issued
The four others for whose arrest warrants have been issued are:
1. Mr. Tao Yin-chi, educator now in America.
2, 3 and 4. Chang Chung-mien, Chen Tac-hung and Chen Chih, members of the National Salvation Association.

Names Signed
The last named three and Ku and Ren, who are now in custody and charged with the eight others, it is understood, were among the 21 National Salvation Association members who visited Soochow in January to appeal to the Kiangsu High Court for a speedy trial and release of their leaders. In submitting the petition, the court authorities asked them to nominate delegates and sign their names on the document. The five signed. Early in February, summons were sent to Shanghai asking the five to appear in court. Ku and Ren attended the session accordingly and were promptly detained. The three others failed to attend and warrants for their arrest have been issued.

Repeated petitions had been sent to Nanking and the court authorities in Soochow asking for their acquittal and immediate release. A few weeks ago, leading American educators, professors and editors jointly sent a telegram to Nanking expressing their concern over the seven National Salvation leaders. It is believed that the court has ordered the arrest of Mr. Tao Yin-chu as result of this telegram, believing that he was the man who prompted the Americans to send the telegram. Several of the signatories of the despatch to Nanking, it is recalled, were professors at Columbia University Teachers' College.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Monday, December 14, 1936

Dementi
To the Editor:
Allow me to inform you that the report which appeared in your esteemed paper of Dec. 8, to the effect that "General Feng Yu-hsiang is harboring Miss Sze Lianz, woman lawyer who jumped bail after being arrested on charge of being a leader of the National Salvation Association," is absolutely groundless. It is a lie, pure and simple.
That the lie was fabricated with a malicious intent can hardly be questioned, since the Japanese paper from which you quoted declared Feng as a "notorious anti-Japanese leader."
Inasmuch as the report in question was a reproduction from the Japanese "Shanghai Nippo" you are of course duty-bound to produce the paper and send it on to us if you please.
Let me say, however, that it is perhaps more correct to say that General Feng is anti-Japanese imperialism and aggression rather than that he is anti-Japanese, for there is a world of difference between the two attitudes. If anti-Japanese imperialism and aggression are considered by the Japanese to be anti-Japanese, then there is no use of debating it here.
Kindly make due correction of the report in your next issue of the Shanghai Evening Post, send me a copy of the Japanese "Shanghai Nippo" in question and have this letter of mine published at the same time.
With greetings and thanking you in advance,
Yours for international good-will,
T. M. LOO.
Secretary of the General
General Feng's Headquarters
Nanking.
Dec. 11, 1936.

We gladly publish the above letter. However, having received the translation in question from a news agency and not being possessed of the copy of the "Nippo" for which demand is made, we have no intention of acting as a free clipping bureau for the General's Headquarters.

Meantime, Miss Sze Liang, the only girl and the seventh member of the group, was still missing yesterday. Arrested in her home two weeks ago during a raid when the other members were also taken into custody in their respective residences, Miss Sze, who is a lawyer by profession, was released on the bond of her attorney.

She failed to appear the next morning when a special session was arranged for the hearing of the arrested Salvation Association leaders at the 3rd Kiangsu High Court. Except for a letter received by her lawyers stating that she had no intention of returning to Shanghai to face trial, the fugitive girl has not been heard of since the day she walked out of the courtroom.

Miss Sze's lawyers were arraigned by the High Court last week for their failure to produce their charge. A court order directed them to furnish bail for their own liberty and produce Miss Sze in Court within 10 days.

In their desperate hope that Miss Sze might return, the attorneys inserted front page advertisements in local Chinese dailies, pleading that she live up to her promises. "LIBERAL", contributing to The Readers'

things upon the detention of six members of

While conscious of our obligation, as a
foreign journal in China, not to indulge in
undue tendering of advice or critical activity
toward the nation which is our host, we feel

contrary has manifested itself, the fact has
not come to our attention.
More pleasant, however, is the fact that

THE CHINA PRESS, FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 27, 1936. No. S. B. D. 2086
Late

Editor, THE CHINA PRESS.
Sir,—I hope you will grant a foreign reader the space to express his views on the reported re-arrest, and your editorial comment thereon, of the National Salvation Association leaders. For a person who has closely followed the events of the last 12 months, it seems unbelievable—if not to say outrageous—that prominent personalities of social standing like the seven arrested should be persecuted for publicly advocating a united patriotic front against foreign aggression. And it appears simply farcical when you state, in this connection that "confronted by external aggression China must of necessity preserve every ounce of her energy in a unified struggle for national existence." If the united front as advocated and achieved by the National Salvation Association is accused of "subversive activities," who shall carry on a united struggle? Is a coalition with Japan the desired "united front" then?
Every right-minded person, familiar with Chinese personalities, knows that the arrested lawyers, bankers, etc. have done nothing but defended the unity and national independence of China, and have found enthusiastic supporters in all the ranks of the Chinese people.
In the light of your statement (in the editorial "Admitted") that the "Chinese are . . . not prepared to yield to military pressure without fighting to the last," the reader must come to the conclusion that you are inconsistent or—worse—biassed.
In the second paragraph of "Subversive" you express your confidence "that justice will be meted out in accordance with law" while in the last paragraph of the same editorial you come to the conclusion that "by agitation . . . they have merely forfeited their right even to a hearing of their views."
Comparing these two statements, one becomes naturally afraid as to the fate of the seven arrested, if the most elementary right of every accused—to be heard—should be violated.
The open support of the strikers in Japanese mills by the National Salvation Association does not prove any instigation. The workers who slave endless hours for a miserable $12 a month need no agitators to tell them which way the wind blows. It was only logical that the strikers should be supported in view of the ten per cent wage-increase granted by Chinese mill-owners.
For a foreigner who believes in the Bill of Rights; who knows furthermore that revolutionary leaders in the fight for national independence like George Washington have found great admiration in China; and who sees the necessity of a really united front among the Chinese people, irrespective of political views, in order to waive off foreign aggression:—the arrests and your comments thereon seem inconsistent with your own views on national unity, nay, even most unpatriotic.
A BRITISH READER.

Mme. Sun Yat-sen (Soong Ching-ling) today issued a vigorous protest against the arrest of members of the Executive Committee of the All-China Federation of National Salvation Associations, at the same time dealing with rumors in the Japanese press that she herself has been arrested by French authorities. Her statement follows in full:
* * *
As one of the members of the Executive Committee of the All-China Federation of National Salvation Associations and in view of the arrest of seven of the leaders of this organization, I wish to enter my protest against these unwarranted arrests and the groundless charges made against them.

Japanese Influence
It is obvious to any thinking person that these arrests and these charges are the result of Japanese influence. That the hand of the Japanese can be seen in these arrests is evidenced by the report of the Shanghai Mainichi, issued on November 25th (yesterday) in which it is stated that I was arrested early this morning by the French authorities, charged with Communist activities, in connection with the Third International. Perhaps the Mainichi and the Nippo, which published similar rumors, have advance information, in which case my contention is well taken!

Contrary to the provocative assertions of the Japanese, the National Salvation Association is neither pro-Communist nor anti-Government. These charges are deliberately fabricated by the Japanese as a means of inciting the Chinese Government against the National Salvation Association, thus driving a wedge between the Chinese Government and the people for their own advantage.

Not Anti-Government
Despite these arrests and malicious charges, the National Salvation Association reaffirms its position: It is not anti-Government; it is not pro-Communist; it is for a united front to all people, regardless of their political beliefs or party affiliations, and for a national war of liberation.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 26, 1936

Charges Against Salvation
Group Suspects Defined

Instigation Of General Strike In Shanghai Is
Alleged By City Government To Have Been
Planned By Seven Arrested Leaders

Reasons for the arrest on Monday morning of seven well-known Shanghai residents and ways of dealing with them were explained in an official statement issued by the Greater Shanghai Municipality yesterday evening.

The seven arrested persons are: Li Kung-po, principal of the Liang Tsai Memorial School, Wang Tsaoshih, professor of Economics at Kwang Hwa University, Miss Shih Liang, attorney, Sha Chien-li, lawyer, Chang Nai-chi, formerly Assistant Manager of the Chekiang Industrial Bank, Shen Chun-ju, dean of the Shanghai Law College, and Tsuo Tao-fen, formerly editor of the "Life Weekly."

A free translation of the statement follows:

"Since the illegal organization of the National Salvation Association under their auspices, Li Kung-po and the others have maliciously manufactured rumours, under the guise of national salvation, their motive being no other than to weaken the people's confidence in the Central Government.

Recently, they have associated themselves with Communists, advocating the formation of the so-called people's united front, instigating class conflict, advocating the substitution of a National Defence Government for the Central Government.

Lenient Attitude

During the past year the authorities have adopted a most lenient attitude toward them, incessantly advising them to give up such activities. All the advice, however, had fallen on deaf ears, and worse, their opinions have recently taken shape in concrete activities.

Substantial evidence has been obtained that they recently have been secretly fanning a general labour strike in Shanghai, in order to attain their objective of creating disturbance and overthrowing the government.

At the present juncture, when the Suiyuan situation is tense, it is imperative that order and peace should be solidly maintained in the rear. To nip destructive forces in the bud, the authorities could not help but adopt the measures as called for in a period of emergency.

Unprecedented Crisis

When the nation is passing through such an unprecedented crisis, it is time that the entire nation, high and low, co-operated. Under such circumstances, it is necessary that subversive activities of a few radicals be curbed.

As to ways of dealing with them, it is natural that they will be tried in accordance with the proper procedure of law.

It has also been discovered that Communistic elements are still included in the National Salvation. To purge the organ of all undesirable influences, representatives have been sent together with members of the City Tangpu, to make a detailed investigation.

Court after the police had found themselves unable to contact the District Court in Nantao to obtain dispatch warrants, which was the proper procedure for arrests to be made on extra-Settlement roads. All four men were residents of extra-Settlement roads.

Voluntarily Surrenders

Messrs. Sheng and Wang were nabbed at 1 o'clock yesterday while at home in bed. Sa was picked up later but apparently was not so badly wanted as the others because he did not appear in court yesterday. Mr. Li, however, managed to evade re-arrest by not staying at home. He was out when the police called, nor did he appear until about 2.45 p.m. yesterday when he made a dramatic entrance into the courtroom and voluntarily gave himself up.

When the four men were released on personal bond Monday afternoon, the next hearing of the case was remanded until Wednesday afternoon. Their re-arrest, however, made it necessary that they be brought before the tribunal yesterday. The session was opened before a full court. A representative of the Bureau of Public Safety presented request for the handing over of the three prisoners on the grounds that their names had been linked with certain communistic activities in China, although admittedly members of the National Salvation Association, which professes to be non-communistic in character.

The representative continued that certain communists had been arrested by the Chinese authorities and that these people had implicated Messrs. Li, Wang and Shen as important members of the radical group. This was denied by the three prisoners.

Mr. Li was the first of the three to speak on his own behalf. He spent little time dwelling on the charges but declared that he had been illegally re-arrested; that the First Special District Court had no right to re-arrest him after he had once been arrested and released on bond. Mr. Shen, a man of short stature but still active despite his 68 years of age, was the second speaker and he also claimed illegal arrest. Mr. Wang followed with a similar claim.

Former Minister Present

The large group of attorneys for the prisoners headed by Mr. Chang Yao-tang, former Minister of Justice for the defunct Peking Government, spent considerable time on the subject of illegal arrest, and further insisted that a prima facie case be established against their clients before extradition could even be considered. They declared that the court could not accept the statement made by the re-

Public Safety as a prima facie case. Further, they demanded that proof to the representative's statements be submitted.

At 3.30 p.m., the court called a recess of five minutes, after which it announced that "since the three resided in Chinese territory off extra-Settlement roads, the question of extradition does not arise."

This announcement had the effect of an exploding bombshell on almost everyone in the courtroom. If such was the case, then the prisoners would automatically become the prisoners of the Bureau of Public Safety. Nothing was said by the court, however, in respect to handing the men over.

The matter did not end here, however. Both the prisoners and their attorneys continued to fight for their freedom and this time, they charged that they had been illegally re-arrested because the warrants had been issued by the First Special District Court and not the Special District Court in Nantao.

Up To Nantao Court

Under the old Mixed Court Rendition Agreement, it was provided that prisoners taken by the Settlement police must be handed over to a modern law court. Since the Nantao court comes under this classification, prisoners are handed over only to that court and not to the Bureau of Public Safety which is a police body. In the case of arrests on extra-Settlement roads, such arrests have been made in the past on despatch warrants issued by the Nantao tribunal and not the First Special District Court.

The court, however, did not take an active part in the discussions that followed on this point. It had already rendered its decision to the effect that no question of extradition had arisen since the arrested men resided in Chinese controlled territory. Despite this ruling, however, the matter of handing the men over had not been settled.

Police officials at the court communicated the turn the proceedings had taken to police headquarters on Foochow Road and asked for instructions. Instructions came back from headquarters, apparently, to hand the men over. This was subsequently announced in court and the police took custody of the trio, bringing an end to the proceedings.

After considerable discussion of this point, the High Court admitted that the warrants should have been issued by the Nantao tribunal and accordingly withdrew the warrants of re-arrest. This action left Messrs. Li, Shen and Wang free men, enjoying the same status they had when they were released under personal bond on Monday.

This situation, however, was short-lived. Settlement police officers in the court-room apparently acting on instructions from their superiors, immediately took custody of the three men, and it was announced that they were to be handed over. The action raised a shout of disapproval from spectators but constables had restored order in a few minutes.

Salvation Trio
Back In Prison
After Release
Three Alleged Chiefs
Enjoy But Brief
Freedom
POLICE PICK UP
MEN AT HOMES
Japanese Circulating
Wild Rumors About
Mass Arrests
After but 12 hours' freedom granted them yesterday when Judge Nylh of the Second Branch Kiangsu High Court released them in the custody of their attorneys, three alleged leaders of the All-China National Salvation Association, described in Chinese government circles as anti-government and subversive, were rearrested early this morning on an authority of a court warrant issued by Judge Nylh.
The men, Mr. Wong Tsao-shih, 34-year-old professor of economics at Kwang Hua University and lawyer, Mr. Shao Chung-ju, dean of the Shanghai Law College and member of the standing committee of the Bar Association, and Mr. So Chine-li, 34-year-old lawyer, were rearrested at their homes at 1 o'clock this morning by Detective-Sergeant Kelly of Bubbling Well Police Station and Detective-Sergeant Haskell of Sinza Station. Mr. Li Kung-po, president of the Tlang Tsai Memorial School, although before the High Court yesterday, was not taken into custody again.
Face Judge Today
All three men were being brought before Judge Nylh this afternoon where an application was being made for their handing over to the Bureau of Public Safety on a charge of committing acts with intent to injure the Republic of China.
Wild rumors concerning the arrest of seven supposed members of the salvation group were circulating about Shanghai this morning with Japanese dailies taking the lead. The Shanghai Nippo advanced the theory that the action of police in arresting the men was precipitated by their activities in the recent strikes in Japanese-owned mills, but this was vehemently denied in official police circles, it being pointed out that the men had simply been arrested at the request of the Bureau of Public Safety and that the Settlement Police had no case against them.
Must Present Case
It was pointed out by members of the legal profession this morning that in order to secure the custody of the three lawyers it would be necessary for the Bureau of Public Safety to present a prima facie case against them and give evidence concerning their supposed participation in subversive activities. If on the other hand, a court dispatch was obtained from the Nanking District Court, such evidence would not be necessary and the men would automatically be handed over.
Claiming that the movements of the National Salvation Association had lately turned from an anti-Japanese character to an anti-Nanking character, the Shanghai Nippo said that the seven leaders arrested yesterday were in some way connected with anti-Japanese terrorist gangs and went on to say that only the arrest of those pulling wires behind a screen of these pulling wires behind a screen of respectability will put an end to the anti-Japanese activities.
Hits F.M.P.
Lashing out against the French authorities, the paper declared that "lukewarm police" made it a paradise for political plotters, members of secret societies and political refugees.
"Connections are maintained between Hongkong and the French Concession here by secret organizations and political groups which have their headquarters in those two areas. In order that these subversive elements may be eliminated, it will be necessary for the French Concession authorities to take drastic suppressive measures.
"Although the Concession authorities seem to be co-operating closely with the S.M.P., the Japanese consular police and the Bureau of Public Safety, they lack determination," the journal charged.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Monday, November 23, 1936
Police Arrest Prominent Leaders Of Local
Salvation Association During Night Raids;
Drag-Net Gets Seven; Court Hearing Slated

Six Men, One
Woman Seized
For Agitation

Publishers, Attorneys
Among Prisoners
Being Held

CHINESE POLICE
ASK EXTRADITION

Sextet Said Warned
Against Activity
Opposing Japan

Seven alleged leaders of the All-China National Salvation Association, described in Chinese official quarters as anti-government, subversive and responsible for the many demonstrations in Shanghai including the agitation for a general strike in Japanese cotton mills, were rounded up by International Settlement and French Concession police early this morning.

The arrests were carried out at the request of the Bureau of Public Safety of the City Government of Greater Shanghai, which is asking the extradition of the seven persons to face possible charges of offenses against the security of the state.

Raids Made Simultaneously
Carrying out the raids simultaneously between 1:30 and 3 o'clock this morning, the police arrested the seven persons in their respective homes. Those arrested in the International Settlement are:

Mr. Li Kung-po, president of the Liang Tsi Industrial School (in charge of Mr. See Liang), publisher of the ... and a returned student from America. He was arrested at his home at 14, Lane 524, Avenue Road. A book in Japanese containing four leaflets, the contents of which were not revealed, was found in his home.

Taken In Frenchtown
The three others arrested in the French Concession are:

Mr. Tsao Tao-feng, formerly editor of the Life Weekly, vernacular magazine which once had the biggest circulation in China and who was forced to be removed from the editorial chair for his anti-government outbursts to make a trip abroad. He was also well-known as an educator. He was arrested at his home at 4, Lane 601, Route Lafayette.

Dr. Tsang Nai-chi, a returned student from America, formerly assistant manager of the Chekiang Industrial Bank and formerly vice-managing director of the Chinese Bankers' Credit Information Bureau. He was arrested at his Rue Delastre home.

Miss Sze Liang, the only woman among the seven. She also is a legal practitioner, being affiliated with the law offices of Attorney Tung Kong, famous Chinese lawyer now lecturing in Peiping and mentioned for membership in the Judicial Committee of the Hopei-Chahar Political Council. She was once wounded in a demonstration at West Gate against the Japanese occupation of Shenyang on September 18, 1931. Officers gained entrance to her home at 1 Lafayette Terrace, Route Lafayette, by climbing over the wall.

All Face Courts
The seven arrested persons, widely known for their agitation for an immediate declaration of war against Japan, today were facing the courts. The four arrested in the Settlement were brought before the Second Branch Kiangsu High Court this morning after the courtroom had been cleared of reporters and persons not directly connected with the case. The hearing was conducted in camera. After a lengthy session, during which the Public Safety Bureau is understood to have requested their extradition, the hearing was adjourned until Wednesday afternoon and the four persons were allowed bail on their personal bonds, signed by their defense attorneys.

The three others, arrested in the French Concession, were facing the Third Branch Kiangsu High Court this afternoon. Similar requests were to be made for their extradition by the Public Safety Bureau, it is understood. Dr. T. Z. Chang was to appear for the defense of Miss Sze Liang and Mr. Tsao Tao-feng.

Movements Watched
Movements of the seven alleged leaders, who also are alleged to be founders of a political party known as the "Popular Front," have long been watched since the outbreak of subversive agitation in Kwangtung and Kwangsi. They are understood to have been repeatedly warned by the Chinese authorities against any anti-Japanese demonstrations in echo of the Kwangtung-Kwangsi demands for war with Japan.

When the labor disputes broke out in Japanese cotton mills, their movements again were kept under close watch. Allegations that they were pouring the oil of political issues into the flames of labor disputes are believed to be the immediate cause for their arrest.

The seven persons also are alleged to be anti-General Chiang Kai-shek, opposing the president of the Executive Yuan and chairman of the Military Affairs Commission with attempting to create a similar regime in China with himself as the dictator.

LOCAL CULTURAL BODIES GIVE ENTHUSIASTIC WELCOME TO KWOH
MEI-SHU AND THREE NATIONAL SALVATION LEADERS

At 2 p.m. yesterday, the Shanghai Cultural
Circles' National Extinction Aversion Association and other
various local cultural bodies held a meeting at the Shang
Wan Primary School (尚文小学) to accord a joint welcome to
Messrs. Kwoh Mei-sheh(郭沫若), Sung Chun-dz (沈钧儒),
Tsang Nai-chi (章乃器) and Li Kung-poh (李公朴). About
1,000 persons were present. Mr. Pan Kung-chan, Commissioner
of the Bureau of Social Affairs, presided.
Mr. Pan Kung-chan delivered an opening
speech, in the course of which he said :- "We are here
to-day to extend our warm welcome to Messrs. Kwoh Mei-sheh,
Sung Chun-dz, Tsang Nai-chi and Li Kung-poh. At this time
when our country is facing an acute alien aggression, every
one of us should cast aside his views and join hands together
to make up a strong body. If we still fail to harmonize
with one another in spirit and action, it will mean suicide
for our country. As our country is now at the cross-roads
of existence or ruin, there is no alternative for us but to
put up a war of resistance. A section of the people is
speculating whether the government will choose war or peace.
Such speculation is entirely out of place. The Chinese
people love peace; not only that, they love peace in the
Far-East as well as in the rest of the world. However, at
present even if we desire peace, others will not permit us
to enjoy it. Moreover, peace can only be assured under
conditions of equality. How can there be peace if there
is still difference? We must keep in mind that the present
war of resistance is to be carried on to the bitter end and
that it will affect all the people. Every one of us should
be prepared for the sacrifice and offer all he has to the
government. The cultural bodies should make the people
understand that the present war is not a childish play; it
is the life and death struggle of our nation. Ordinary
people should not doubt nor interfere with the government
in its handling of the situation or its tactics of war.
We must have full confidence in our government and leader
to handle the delicate situation. The cultural circles
should make preparations to organize and train the people,
so that the people may not be surprised when a great war c
commences."
In reply, Mr. Kwoh Mei-sheh said:- "I am
greatly honoured at the enthusiastic welcome given to me.
It is my opinion that words are unnecessary if a war of
resistance is to be put up. It depends entirely on action.
All of us, the cultural, agricultural, industrial and
commercial circles, should participate in the present war
of resistance. In the past we had no determination because
of our respect for life and property. I can say that we
shall thwart our enemy if all of us will readily sacrifice
our lives and property. We must do our best in the present
war of resistance under the guidance of our highest leader."
Speeches were also delivered by Messrs. Sung
Chun-dz, Tsang Nai-chi and Li Kung-poh, all of whom expressed
the hope that the government would organize the people and
that the people would be united in spirit and movement.

IMPROVED MEASURES OF REGISTERING RICSHA COOLIES

The S.M.C. has never before enquired whether the public ricsha coolies registered with it actually engage in ricsha pulling. JAPANESE AUTHORITIES TO SUPPRESS HEROIN DEALERS

The Chinese authorities are adopting effective measures in the suppression of opium smokers and heroin dealers and they are obtaining satisfactory results.

In view of the fact that quite a number of Japanese subjects, mostly Koreans, in the North are engaged in the heroin business, the Japanese authorities are reported to have decided to adopt effective measures to suppress them. As a result, Chinese, White Russians, Koreans and Japanese who are dealing in heroin in the North are retreating to Shanghai. In view of this, the local Japanese Consular Police are reported to have decided to co-operate with the Chinese Police Bureau, the S.M.P. and the French Police to adopt severe repressive measures. At present persons coming to Shanghai by train or steamer are liable to arrest if suspected. The majority of the arrested persons are reported to be Koreans. Persons charged for the first time with dealing in heroin are fined and deported to Korea and persons who have previous convictions on a similar charge are sentenced to imprisonment. However, many of those who were sent to Korea are coming back to Shanghai because they cannot make a living there. Therefore the Japanese authorities are now considering suitable measures to deal with them.
